extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, playwrights, and readers of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging classical tragedy (Aristotelian poetics): definition of tragedy, its parts, their relative importance, and principles of plot construction (unity, magnitude, probability, reversal, recognition, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished (rhythm, harmony, and song), in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that language be 'embellished' (some parts in verse, others aided by song). The aim is to arouse pity and fear and bring about their proper purgation. Tragedy imitates action (not merely men) and represents what may happen according to probability or necessity rather than merely what has happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (temporal restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: As far as possible, Tragedy should confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (a single day); Epic has no limits of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temporal limitation is historically typical of tragedy (competition/performance context) though flexibility existed early on; it helps maintain unity and perspicuity of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Constituent Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality—namely, Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of the parts (Song, Diction) constitute the medium of imitation, one (Diction) the manner, and three (Plot, Character, Thought) the objects of imitation. All plays contain these elements though some appear more prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority / Relative Importance of the Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is most important (the soul of tragedy); Character is second in importance; Thought third; Diction (expression) follows; Song is the chief embellishment; Spectacle is least artistic and least connected with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot (the arrangement of incidents) determines tragic effect; spectacle's effects depend more on the stage machinist than the poet. Novices often achieve diction and portraiture before constructing plot; still the plot is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as Imitation of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the imitation of the action: by plot is meant the arrangement of the incidents. Dramatic action, not character, is the principal thing—action is necessary for tragedy; there may be tragedy without character but not without action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is subsidiary to action because actions determine joy or suffering. A set of well-finished speeches alone will not produce the essential tragic effect if the plot and incidents are not artistically constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole / Completeness of Plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'whole' has a beginning (which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity), a middle (which follows and is followed), and an end (which naturally follows other things but has nothing following it). A well-constructed plot must conform to these principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard; each part should follow by necessity or probability from what precedes. The proper structure preserves causal or probable succession among parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (proper length)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be of a certain magnitude: neither too small (confused, imperceptible) nor too large (eye cannot take it all in; unity lost); proper magnitude is such that the whole can be embraced by memory and allows a change from good to bad fortune or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty depends on magnitude and order. Roughly, the magnitude should admit a sequence of events (by probability/necessity) that will allow a change of fortune (peripeteia) and still be perspicuous to the spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (structural organicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in imitating one action that is whole: the structural union of parts should be such that if any one is displaced or removed the whole will be disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is not unity of the hero (one man) but unity of action; a hero's many adventures do not guarantee unity. The plot should center on a single unified action with necessary/probable connections among incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Episodic (epeisodic) Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An epeisodic plot is one in which episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets create episodic pieces (often to please players or stretch plots for show); good plots maintain continuity where incidents follow by probability or necessity rather than arbitrary succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the Possible (probability and necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (and tragedy) should represent what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity, not merely what has happened (history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's work is to relate what is possible and universal (how a person of a certain type will act), not merely particular historical events. Credibility rests on possibility; what has happened is manifestly possible, but the poet may invent plausible events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and Causal Order (best effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that produce pity and fear work best when they come by surprise while also following as cause and effect; tragic wonder is heightened when events appear designed rather than accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the statue of Mitys falling and killing his murderer—coincidences are most striking when they have an air of design. Plots constructed so that surprising outcomes are causally grounded are superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple (change of fortune without reversal or recognition) or Complex (change accompanied by Reversal of the Situation and/or Recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with peripeteia or anagnorisis) are generally superior because reversal and recognition heighten emotional interest; these moments should arise from the internal logic of the plot so that effects follow from antecedent causes/probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, always subject to probability or necessity (example: in Oedipus the messenger comes to free Oedipus but instead produces the opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reversal should be produced by the plot's internal structure and lead to increased pity/fear. It is most effective when coincident with Recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined to good or bad fortune; best when coincident with Reversal of the Situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition may occur in various forms (persons, discovery of who did something, even inanimate tokens). When combined with reversal it produces the strongest tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character defined and subordinated
rubrics_metrics.description: Character means that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; it reveals moral purpose (what a man chooses or avoids). Character is subsidiary to action—actions determine outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches must make moral purpose manifest; speeches that do not show choice/avoidance are not expressive of character. A tragedy can lack fine portraiture yet have powerful effect if the plot is well constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (reasoning and thematic content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; it includes where something is proved or a general maxim is enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In oratory thought corresponds to political art/rhetoric; in tragedy it appears in the utterance of general truths or arguments that suit the situation and reveal reasoning appropriate to character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose. It is the medium/manner by which imitation is effected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should be appropriate to the parts of the play; rhythm, harmony, and song enter into the language. Diction is important but subordinate to plot and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song as Chief Embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds chief place among the embellishments of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song contributes to the decorative and emotional qualities of the piece; some parts of a play are rendered through verse alone, others with song.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle's Limited Artistic Value
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has emotional attraction of its own but is the least artistic part and least connected with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power of tragedy is felt even apart from representation and actors; spectacular effects depend more on the stage machinist than the poet. Thus spectacle should not be relied upon as the central artistic source of tragic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructional Origin of Reversal and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia and Recognition are parts of the plot and the most powerful elements of emotional interest; they must arise from the internal structure of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their occurrence should be the necessary or probable result of preceding actions, not arbitrary artifices; when properly built into plot they determine the issues of good or bad fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Ordering and Economy of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful (dramatic) whole must have orderly arrangement of parts and be of a magnitude easily embraced in one view; order and economy contribute to perspicuity and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many disconnected incidents (even if about one man) spoil unity. The poet should be a 'maker of plots' not merely of verses; unify incidents so each part matters to the whole.
